title: Malaysia: Only 14% of Malaysian motorists have flood insurance cover for their vehicles despite rising disaster losses - Asia Insurance Review
text: Malaysia: Only 14% of Malaysian motorists have flood insurance cover for their vehicles despite rising disaster losses By Anoop Khanna" /> --> Advanced Search Subscribe | Newsletter | Sitemap Toggle navigation Home Magazine News Asia China China CEO C-Suite Non-Life Life and Health People Regional Regulations Reinsurance Risk Management Technology Agents Middle East AIR+ Archives AIR Archives Conference Dailies Supplements Press Release Conferences Awards Asia Industry Awards Rolls of Honour Middle East Industry Awards Trusted Life Agents Awards Global Insurance Excellence Awards Calendar Calendar 2026 Calendar 2027 Advertise eDirectory Products Contact Us Get the full experience with our app Read in App News Non-Life 16 Nov 2026 Malaysia: Only 14% of Malaysian motorists have flood insurance cover for their vehicles despite rising disaster losses By Anoop Khanna | 16 Nov 2026 Related News Malaysia: Insurers see long-term risks from climate change though sector out­look still positive Australia: Majority reject hikes in housing insurance premiums Australia: Insurers back Victoria's mandatory flood planning rules Malaysia: Potential MS&AD-LPI deal could create Malaysia's largest general insurer South Asia: Climate change can expose millions to the risk of migration Malaysia Property & Casualty Claims Despite Malaysia's high flood risk, optional flood coverage adoption remains critically low sitting at just 14% for motor policies and 33% for fire and property policies, according to General Insurance Association of Malaysia (PIAM). According to data published by Malaysian Ministry of Transport, there are 40.77m registered vehicles of which 26.6m are actively on the road. However, around 87% of these active vehicles face the risk of significant losses, as they have not opted for flood insurance coverage. PIAM CEO Mr Chua Kim Soon has said the low take-up of flood covers is a matter of serious concern given the scale of flood losses in the country. Mr Chua was addressing a recent media briefing organised by PIAM. The briefing focussed on “Monsoon Risks, Protection and Recovery”. The session highlighted the importance of understanding and preparing for monsoon-related risks, while raising awareness of the role insurance plays in protecting lives and livelihood and supporting recovery in the aftermath of unforeseen events. According to data released by the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), flood damage cost the country MYR933.4m ($228.43m) in 2024, with another MYR636.9m recorded in losses in 2025. Mr Chua said vehicle and property owners should check their policies rather than assume they were automatically covered against natural disasters. He said the protection is not necessarily included in standard policies. Motorists with comprehensive insurance, for instance, generally need to purchase an additional extension to cover flood damage. DOSM data showed that flood-related losses represented 0.03% of nominal GDP in 2025, compared with 0.05% in 2024. PIAM CEO said the threat was not confined to flooding, with Malaysia also recording more than 100 landslide incidents annually and thousands of cases involving fallen trees during thunderstorms. He said changing weather patterns also add to the challenge, with flash floods increasingly occurring outside the usual monsoon period. Mr Chua said PIAM does not propose making flood insurance compulsory for property and vehicle owners. He said the decision should remain with policyholders based on their individual exposure to risk and financial means.
